extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, political thinkers, and reformers interested in culture, religion, and public policy (Victorian/general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing practical political and social operations (bills, reforms, disestablishments) through the lens of culture, reason, and moral development rather than mere mechanical or party-maximizing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culture as method and aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Culture is 'simply the enabling ourselves, whether by reading, observing, or thinking, to come as near as we can to the firm intelligible law of things, and thus to get a basis for a less confused action and a more complete perfection than we have at present.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Culture generates 'a fuller harmonious development of our humanity, a free play of thought upon our routine notions, spontaneity of consciousness, sweetness and light.' It is the preferred means for finding lasting truth and for correcting one-sided or mechanical habits; not to be confounded with mere bookishness or pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground operations in right reason and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in right reason can we get a source of sure authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical operations and state measures should be justified by reason and justice rather than by partisan impulses or mechanical maxims; reason and justice are persuasive and can win lasting assent where fetishistic rules cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on mechanical maxims or fetishes
rubrics_metrics.description: An operation performed in virtue of a mechanical rule, or fetish, ... does not easily inspire respect in its adversaries, and make their opposition feeble and hardly to be persisted in, as an operation evidently done in virtue of reason and justice might.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies driven by stock notions (e.g., 'national mind' formulas, blanket maxims against establishments) provoke counter-fetishes, heighten hostility, and fail to conciliate; prefer reflective consideration of motives and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek persuasion and conciliation (win the affections)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the main benefits to be got by operating on the Irish Church is to win the affections of the Irish people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A just and reasonable operation should be framed so as to enlist goodwill and understanding; operations pursued solely to satisfy a fetish will not awaken love and gratitude and will provoke stronger resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish individual thought from collective worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought and knowledge ... is eminently an individual matter, and of our own; the more we possess it as strictly of our own, the more power it has on us. Man worships best, therefore, with the community; he philosophises best alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public worship benefits from publicity, external manifestation, antiquity and collective observance; policies about religion should preserve collective, public forms of worship while leaving intellectual and speculative matters as individual as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure suitability of state religious arrangements by common-reason apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Property assigned for the purpose of providing for a people's religious worship when that worship was one, the State should, when that worship is split into several forms, apportion between those several forms, with due regard to circumstances, taking account only of great differences, which are likely to be lasting, and of considerable communions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State ought to be 'of the religion of all its citizens, without the fanaticism of any of them.' Apportionment should consider lasting, significant religious differences but overlook petty or transitory splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult living consciousness rather than abstract stock notions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unsafe and misleading to say that our children have rights against us; what is true and safe to say is, that we have duties towards our children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy ideas derived from abstract reasoning about 'rights' should be tested against immediate moral consciousness and duties; do not assume formalized rights automatically yield practical or moral efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer cultural, gradual methods over abrupt legal fixes for deep habits
rubrics_metrics.description: A free disinterested play of thought ... is a thousand times more really practical, a thousand times more likely to lead to some effective result, than an operation such as [immediate legislative reform].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep social habits (e.g., feudal land succession) are better dissolved by gradual persuasion, education, and culture ('sweetness and light') than by abrupt statutory operations that lack persuasive moral basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess reforms by effects on both targeted group's welfare and the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the perpetuation of such a class is for its own real welfare and for the real welfare of the community, depends on the actual circumstances of this class and of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing reforms (e.g., inheritance law), consider both how changes affect the subject group's character and welfare and how they influence the broader social fabric; one-size-fits-all 'natural rights' fixes may be counterproductive in certain historical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let partisan alliances determine just policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual power ... by virtue of which the Liberal party in the House of Commons is now trying to disestablish the Irish Church, is not the power of reason and justice, it is the power of the Nonconformists' antipathy to Church establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware policies driven primarily by political coalition pressures or interest-group antipathies rather than by impartial consideration of justice and reason; such motivations undermine moral authority and future stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uncritical scriptural literalism (Hebraising) in statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: For Liberal statesmen to Hebraise is surely unsafe, and to see poor old Liberal hacks Hebraising ... is even painful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State policy should not adopt literal or unexamined religious maxims as absolute political rules; religious texts may inform moral thought but must be critically integrated with reason and practical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance liberty with renouncement; perfect freedom is service
rubrics_metrics.description: We no more allow absolute validity to [the maxim] 'Liberty is the law of human life,' than we allow it to the opposite maxim, which is just as true, 'Renouncement is the law of human life.' For we know that the only perfect freedom is, as our religion says, a service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and moral judgment should weigh individual liberty against the value of self-discipline and service to higher human perfection; simplistic maxim 'liberty above all' is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring maxims into the movement of thought to test and vitalize them
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose we try and make our consciousness bathe and float this piece of petrifaction,--for such it now is,--and bring it within the stream of the vital movement of our thought, and into relation with the whole intelligible law of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than accepting maxims as petrified rules, subject them to reflective thought and relate them to broader principles; this may either vindicate them or dissolve them and replace them with sounder motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer motives that create lasting truth over immediate tactical advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: May not the man who promotes this [Hellenising thought] be giving the best help towards finding some lasting truth to minister to the diseased spirit of his time ... ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing whether to join a practical operation, consider whether one's contribution fosters longer-term cultural and moral improvement (lasting truth) rather than merely securing short-term tactical gains.
